reason: The sources provide 15 verified claims across five distinct sites, supporting a detailed narrative about Theia's collision and its remnants inside Earth.
story: 4.5 billion years ago, the early Solar System was a demolition derby. A Mars-sized planet named Theia shared an orbit with the infant Earth until gravity sent it on a suicide mission. The two worlds collided with such violence that they nearly vaporized. While the resulting debris ring eventually formed the Moon, Earth didn't just survive the impact—it effectively ate its attacker. Scientists now believe Earth’s unusually high density is the result of absorbing Theia’s massive iron core. More shockingly, seismic 'CAT scans' have revealed two continent-sized 'blobs' of dense material sitting 1,800 miles beneath our feet. These anomalies, located deep under Africa and the Pacific Ocean, are thought to be the bruised remains of Theia’s mantle, buried near Earth’s core for eons. We are living on a chimeric world made from the wreckage of a lost planet.
angle: The 'dead' planet Theia is still inside us—scientists found two continent-sized chunks of it buried 1,800 miles deep in Earth's mantle.

claims.claim: Theia was a Mars-sized protoplanet that collided with Earth approximately 4.5 billion years ago.
The debris ejected from this collision re-coalesced to form the Moon.
The Moon and Earth share nearly identical isotopic compositions, suggesting they are made of the same material.
The impact occurred between 20 million and 100 million years after the Solar System began to form.
New high-resolution simulations suggest the Moon may have formed in only a matter of hours.
Theia is theorized to have had a metallic iron core and a rocky mantle.
Theia's iron core likely sank into and merged with the Earth's core, explaining Earth's high density.
Two continent-sized anomalies called Large Low-Velocity Provinces exist at the base of Earth's mantle.
These mantle 'blobs' are thousands of miles wide and make up about 6% of the Earth's volume.
Seismic evidence and simulations suggest these blobs are remnants of Theia's mantle buried inside Earth.
The Moon is depleted in volatile elements compared to Earth because they vaporized during the impact.
Iron and molybdenum isotopes currently in Earth's mantle were likely delivered by Theia's impact.
Theia may have been the primary source of the water found on Earth today.
Advanced high-resolution computer modeling is required to see the immediate formation of the Moon.
The energy from the collision was so great that it likely created a global ocean of magma on Earth.

disputed: The exact impact angle: older models suggest a glancing blow, while newer evidence suggests a head-on collision; the script should attribute this shift to recent studies.
The origin of Theia: some sources suggest it formed at Earth's Lagrange points, while others suggest it migrated from the inner or outer solar system.
The Moon's material source: one model suggests 80% comes from Earth, while another suggests 70-90% comes from Theia; the script should note these are competing simulation results.
Moon formation timeline: traditional theories suggest months or years, but recent NASA simulations propose it formed in hours.
